items.prompt: Why do databases size each B-tree node to one disk page?
hints: What is the cost of reading a node from disk?
A disk reads a whole page at a time.
One node = one page read, and filling the page with keys makes the tree as short as possible.

options.text: Reading a node costs one page read, and a full page of keys keeps the tree short
options.feedback: Right. More keys per node means more children and fewer levels.

options.text: So the tree only ever has one level
options.feedback: A large table still needs a few levels, just far fewer than a binary tree.

options.text: Because each page can hold only one key
options.feedback: A page holds many keys. That is the point of a B-tree.

items.prompt: What does a B+ tree do differently from a B-tree?
hints: In a B+ tree, internal nodes only guide the search.
All records are in the leaves, and the leaves are linked in order.

options.text: It keeps every record in the leaves and links the leaves together
options.feedback: Yes. That is why most databases use B+ trees.

options.text: It lets leaves sit on different levels
options.feedback: B+ trees keep every leaf on the same level too.

options.text: Its nodes have at most two children
options.feedback: That would be a binary tree. B+ tree nodes have many children.

items.prompt: Which query does a B+ tree handle especially well, thanks to its linked leaves?
hints: What can you do once you are standing on one leaf?
The leaves are linked in sorted order.
Find the first key once, then walk along the leaves: a range query.

options.text: A range query, such as all marks from 50 to 60
options.feedback: Right. Search for 50 once, then follow the links until you pass 60.

options.text: The average of all keys, without reading any of them
options.feedback: Every key still has to be read to average them.

options.text: Finding a key without reading any nodes
options.feedback: Every search reads at least one node per level.
